component_findings.dependency_declaration: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Direct dependencies can be declared explicitly at an appropriate project/module boundary rather than inferred from ambient state. Evidence basis: Evaluates language-level dependency semantics: how simply a Swift program declares, resolves, and isolates dependencies at the language/toolchain level (not package-manager maturity, which is Ecosystem). | Based on static analysis of provided template programs and documented Swift language semantics; no live network access for further comparative trials. | Swift programs in template/programs/swift/micro (mb00-mb11) and adversarial (ADV-*) are single-file or few-file programs compiled directly via swiftc with no external package dependencies; mb00.swift is a 15-byte trivial program, others use only the standard library and occasionally Foundation. | Swift's module system (explicit `import X`) provides clean namespace-scoped dependencies at the language level: no header files, no preprocessor, no implicit global includes. | Access control keywords (public/internal/private/fileprivate/open) cleanly separate what a module/dependency exposes, avoiding accidental transitive coupling. | SwiftPM integrates dependency declaration (Package.swift) as executable Swift code in the toolchain, giving one coherent language-to-build-graph story. | Foundation is a separate library from the core standard library, historically rooted in the Objective-C runtime; on non-Darwin platforms this requires linking swift-corelibs-foundation, adding a layer of dependency conditionality not present in langua…

component_findings.artifact_source_separation: Recertified level 3 under the current criterion: Source-level program meaning is not unnecessarily tied to a single compiler ABI, filesystem convention or host-specific build assumption. Evidence basis: Evaluates whether Swift's language specification and standard library are designed abstractly from a specific OS/ABI, independent of how many platforms are currently supported (breadth is Ecosystem). | Assessed via language specification knowledge and structure of provided programs; no cross-platform compilation trials were run in this sandbox (single toolchain image, no network). | Swift's core language (syntax, generics, protocols, value semantics, ARC) is platform-neutral by design and implemented on LLVM, enabling multiple target architectures. | Swift's history and much of its standard-library-adjacent design (Foundation, Objective-C bridging, `NSObject` interop) originated tightly coupled to Apple's runtime and ABI. | On non-Darwin platforms Swift relies on swift-corelibs-foundation / swift-corelibs-xctest reimplementations, so common code frequently needs `#if os(...)` / `#if canImport(Foundation)` conditionals -- a language-level portability-design gap rather than pure ecosystem breadth. | Swift has a stable module ABI only on Apple/Darwin platforms; on Linux/Windows, ABI stability guarantees are weaker, so binary interop is not uniform across platforms by design. | Swift Concurrency (async/await, actors) is specified in the language itself (platform neutral) but its runtime integrates with platform-specific threading/scheduling facilities, requiring per-OS runtime port…
